tagline: Causeways and beach roads trace the making of Jones Beach.
intro: The Historic Parkways of Long Island link woodland driving with causeways and barrier-island beaches. NYSDOT lists six selected scenic parkways: Bethpage, Wantagh, Meadowbrook, Loop, Bay and Ocean. The Ocean Parkway follows Jones Beach Island for 15.59 miles between Jones Beach State Park and Captree State Park. Its lanes pass beachfronts, bayside residences and a wide grassy median in Gilgo State Park. Bethpage runs through the forests of Massapequa Preserve; the Loop crosses marshy Alder Island and uses a drawbridge over Long Creek. Through Jones Beach State Park, the Ocean and Bay parkways run parallel beside the recreation facilities.

Robert Moses and the Long Island State Park Commission built the first section of the Wantagh specifically to bring vehicles to Jones Beach. The causeway and park opened together on August 4, 1929. Creating the park meant raising Jones Island with sand dredged from the bay bottom, then planting beach grass by hand to hold the dunes.

For a west-to-east coastal drive, start where the Meadowbrook meets the Ocean Parkway at Jones Beach. Continue to the water-tower traffic circle at the Wantagh, then past Tobay Beach to West Gilgo and Gilgo Beach. Beyond Gilgo State Park, the road reaches Oak Beach and then Captree, ending just past the Robert Moses Causeway.
notice: Ocean Parkway circles the water tower where the Wantagh reaches Jones Beach.

moments.title: Jones Beach State Park
moments.text: A water tower occupies the traffic circle where the Wantagh meets the Ocean Parkway. Moses made the Italianate tower a central feature of Jones Beach, giving a working structure a conspicuous place in the park’s design. The two bathhouses received equally deliberate attention: he chose Herbert Magoon’s designs and specified Ohio Sandstone and Barbizon brick. The 188-foot tower was modeled on the bell tower of St Mark’s Basilica in Venice and underwent restoration in 2010. The park also has a two-mile boardwalk, with ocean-facing beaches and a separate beach on Zachs Bay.
moments.notice: The Italianate water tower forms the centerpiece of its traffic circle.

moments.title: Gilgo
moments.text: Several houses at West Gilgo arrived by barge from High Hill Beach. Moving them made room for Jones Beach State Park. The Gilgo communities occupy Jones Beach Island, with West Gilgo followed eastward by Gilgo Beach and Cedar Beach. Along this stretch, the Ocean Parkway passes beachfront residences at West Gilgo and bayside homes at Gilgo Beach. At Gilgo Beach, a pedestrian tunnel connects the parking lot with the beach. Beyond the beach access, the road enters Gilgo State Park and its median widens into grass. The homes in these communities are privately owned, but the land is leased from New York State.

moments.title: Oak Beach
moments.text: Ferries from Babylon helped make Oak Beach a cottage community before road travel changed its character. By the first decade of the twentieth century, a lifesaving station stood here, beyond overland reach. Ocean Parkway improved access by car, but Oak Beach remained largely a summer community until the Robert Moses Causeway made travel from mainland Long Island faster. Most residents now live here year-round. The community lies near Jones Beach Island’s eastern end, between the Atlantic Ocean and Great South Bay. Gilgo State Park borders the community to the west; Captree State Park is on its eastern side.
